title: Clearance: take the threat away
outcomes: Names the threat of a vacating move before relying on the line it opens
Predicts what happens to a clearance when its check or its follow-up piece is taken away
Tells a clearance that still works after a change from one that no longer does

steps.text: This lesson builds on **Clearance: step aside with a threat** and **Clearance: win, mate, or only retreat?**. A clearance needs a vacating move the opponent must answer, and a line that leads somewhere. Test it by *removal*: take the threat away in your head, or the piece that would use the line. If the opponent gets a free move, or the line leads nowhere, the idea fails.

steps.caption: Black to move. The rook on f5 stands in front of its own queen.

line.say: Rf1+ is check, so White has no time to cover f3.
The queen travels down the cleared file: Qf3 is mate.

claims.statement: The engine's best move is Rf1+ (depth 16).
After Rf1 the rook gives check to the king on h1.
Rf1+ forces checkmate in 2 or fewer against the engine's best defence.

steps.text:
**The removal test.**
**1.** Name the threat of the vacating move: a check, a capture, or an attack on something bigger.
**2.** Name what the opened line reaches.
**3.** Remove one of them and ask: does the opponent now have a free move to cover?
**Rule of thumb:** a vacating move with no forcing threat usually hands the opponent a free move, and the clearance fails.

steps.title: Same clearance, one change at a time
steps.prompt: Each position changes one thing about the working position (rook on e2, Qxf6 check). Predict whether the queen move still wins, then check.
When you took the threat away in your head, which part was hardest to judge: whether the move was still forcing, or whether a piece still stood behind the one that moved?
